context.text: Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople from 428, took offense at the beloved title Theotokos, 'God-bearer', for the Virgin: Mary bore the man united to the Word, he taught, so call her Christotokos. Cyril of Alexandria saw the stakes at once: if Mary did not bear God, then the one who died on the cross was not God, and we are not saved.

narrative.text: After an exchange of letters in which Cyril set out the faith, the Word did not indwell a man but became man, so that the incarnate Word is one, and his mother is rightly Theotokos, both sides appealed to Rome, and Celestine sided with Cyril. The emperor summoned a council to Ephesus for Pentecost 431.

When John of Antioch's party delayed, the council opened under Cyril on June 22, read Nestorius's writings against the creed of Nicaea, and deposed him the same day, to torchlit rejoicing in the streets of Ephesus, the city of the Virgin. The late-arriving Antiochenes held a rival synod; two years of painful negotiation followed until the Formula of Reunion (433) united Cyril and John in confessing one Christ, perfect God and perfect man, and Mary as Theotokos.
The council also decreed that no one may 'produce or compose another faith' beside that of Nicaea, the canon the Orthodox East would later cite against the filioque's insertion into the creed.

significance.text: Ephesus fixed forever the grammar of the Incarnation: the child of Mary is God the Word himself, one person, and every honor the Church pays the Theotokos guards that confession about her Son. The Orthodox veneration of Mary stands on this council.
